questions.stem: A weak acid drug with a pKa of 4.4 is in gastric juice at pH 1.4. What is the approximate ratio of unionized to ionized drug?
questions.explanation: pKa − pH = 4.4 − 1.4 = 3 = log(HA/A⁻), so HA : A⁻ = 10³ : 1. When pH < pKa, a weak acid is mostly unionized. A: Inverts the ratio; that would apply to a weak base, or to an acid at pH 7.4. B: A difference of 3 log units is 1000, not 100. D: Subtracting the values without taking the antilog. E: 1 : 1 only when pH = pKa.

questions.stem: A patient arrives after an overdose of phenobarbital, a weak acid that is renally excreted. Which intervention will most increase its urinary elimination?

options.A: Ammonium chloride to acidify the urine
options.E: IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine

questions.explanation: Alkaline urine ionizes a weak acid, so it can't be reabsorbed across the tubule (ion trapping) and is excreted. A: Acidifying the urine keeps weak acids unionized → more reabsorption, less elimination. B: Metoclopramide speeds gastric emptying; it doesn't affect renal elimination. C: Fluid restriction lowers urine flow. D: Calcium carbonate acts in the gut and doesn't meaningfully trap the drug in urine.

questions.stem: An oral drug has a bioavailability (F) of 20% and a hepatic extraction ratio (ER) of 0.75. What fraction of the dose is absorbed from the gut (f)?
questions.explanation: F = f × (1 − ER) → 0.20 = f × 0.25 → f = 0.80. A: 0.20 × 0.75 multiplies F by ER, the wrong operation. C: 25% is (1 − ER), not f. D: 0.20 × 0.25 multiplies by (1 − ER) instead of dividing. E: Divides F by ER instead of by (1 − ER).

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?

options.A: It can move drug against its concentration gradient using energy
options.D: It is used by glucose and amino acids
options.E: It occurs at the blood–brain barrier

questions.explanation: Active transport uses energy (ATP) and doesn't need a concentration gradient; facilitated diffusion moves only down the gradient with no energy. B: Both are carrier-mediated. C: Both are saturable. D: Glucose and amino acids are the lecture's examples of facilitated diffusion. E: Carrier-mediated transport of both kinds occurs at the BBB.

questions.stem: A patient has an acute angina attack. Oral nitroglycerin has a bioavailability of only ~10% because of first-pass metabolism. Which route gives the fastest effective relief?
questions.explanation: Sublingual absorption drains into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver, and nitroglycerin acts within 2–3 minutes. B: Transdermal also avoids first pass, but absorption is very slow; patches are for prevention, not acute attacks. A, D, E: All oral forms pass through the portal circulation, so ~90% is destroyed before reaching the systemic circulation; SR and enteric coating also delay onset.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old starts an oral drug that normally undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism. Compared with a young adult, how is the oral bioavailability likely to change?

options.A: Decreased, because gastric emptying is faster
options.B: Increased, because first-pass metabolism is reduced
options.C: Decreased, because gastric acid is increased
options.D: Unchanged, because first-pass metabolism doesn't change with age
options.E: Decreased, because slower GI motility shortens absorption time

questions.explanation: In the elderly ↓ first-pass metabolism → ↑ bioavailability. A: GI motility is decreased in the elderly, not faster. C: Gastric acid is decreased in the elderly, not increased. D: First-pass metabolism declines with age. E: Slower motility lengthens absorption time.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman takes levothyroxine with breakfast together with her calcium supplement. After 3 months she is still hypothyroid. What is the best advice?

options.A: Double the levothyroxine dose and keep the same timing
options.B: Take it with the largest meal of the day instead
options.C: Crush the tablet and take it with a glass of milk
options.D: Take it fasting, 30 min before breakfast, apart from calcium
options.E: Replace the calcium supplement with an antacid at breakfast

questions.explanation: Food and calcium reduce levothyroxine absorption; timing and separation fix the problem. A medication failure is often an absorption or interaction issue, not the drug. A: Raising the dose ignores the interaction. B: More food further reduces absorption. C: Milk adds calcium. E: Antacids also bind and reduce absorption.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with acne has no improvement after 2 months of oral doxycycline. She takes each dose with a glass of milk and an antacid for stomach upset. What best explains the treatment failure?

options.A: Chelation of the drug by divalent cations, reducing absorption
options.D: Increased plasma protein binding of the drug
options.E: Bacterial resistance due to efflux pumps

questions.explanation: Tetracyclines (and fluoroquinolones) bind Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ and Fe²⁺ in the gut, forming poorly absorbed chelates. B: Calcium doesn't induce CYP3A4. C: No P-gp induction occurs here. D: Milk doesn't change plasma protein binding. E: Resistance is possible but doesn't explain the clear interaction with milk and antacids.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and large portosystemic collaterals develops marked toxicity from his usual oral dose of a drug with a high hepatic extraction ratio. The IV dose has never caused problems. What best explains this?

options.A: Reduced gut absorption from bowel-wall edema
options.E: Increased oral bioavailability because portal blood bypasses the liver

questions.explanation: Shunting lets absorbed drug skip first-pass extraction, so oral F rises sharply while the IV dose (no first pass) is unaffected. A: Reduced absorption would lower levels. B: Increased renal clearance would lower levels. C: Enzyme induction would lower levels. D: Slower emptying delays absorption but doesn't raise total exposure this much.

questions.stem: A patient needs a faster onset from an oral analgesic tablet. Which co-administered factor would most speed its delivery to the duodenum for absorption?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide accelerates gastric emptying, delivering the drug sooner to the upper small intestine, the main absorption site. B: Anticholinergics slow gastric emptying. C: Morphine slows gastric emptying. D: Hot drinks slow emptying; cold drinks speed it. E: Intensive exercise slows emptying; moderate exercise speeds it.
